{{short description|Property of equilateral triangles}}
[[File:Satz von van schooten.svg|thumb|upright=0.75|<math>|PA| = |PB| + |PC|</math>]]
'''Van Schooten's theorem''', named after the Dutch mathematician [[Frans van Schooten]], describes a property of [[equilateral triangle]]s. It states:

: ''For an equilateral triangle <math>\triangle ABC</math> with a point <math>P</math> on its [[circumcircle]] the length of longest of the three line segments {{tmath|PA}}, {{tmath|PB}}, {{tmath|PC}} connecting <math>P</math> with the vertices of the triangle equals the sum of the lengths of the other two.''

The theorem is a consequence of [[Ptolemy's theorem]] for [[cyclic quadrilateral]]s. Let <math>a</math> be the side length of the equilateral triangle <math>\triangle ABC</math> and <math>PA</math> the longest line segment. The triangle's vertices together with <math>P</math> form a cyclic quadrilateral {{nobr|<math>\square ABPC</math>.}} By Ptolemy's theorem,
: <math>
|BC| \cdot |PA| = |AC| \cdot |PB| + |AB| \cdot |PC|.
</math>
But, since the triangle is equilateral, {{nobr|<math>|BC| = |AC| = |AB| = a</math>,}} so
: <math>\begin{align}
a \cdot |PA| &= a \cdot |PB| + a \cdot |PC| \\[3mu]
|PA| &= |PB| + |PC|.
\end{align}</math>
